claims.text: EDB-Bio is a scientific reasoning benchmark built from real-world data in three biological domains: drug-perturbation transcriptomics, CRISPR screens, and human GWAS.
Each of EDB-Bio's 96k episodes presents a sequence of experimental results from published studies and asks the model to predict the probability that a target hypothesis is true.
Out-of-the-box open-weight and frontier models show systematic underconfidence and attain Brier scores comparable to a trivial base-rate forecaster.
Post-training against strictly proper scoring rules significantly improves both calibration and discrimination.
In a sequential experiment selection task, the authors' Ibis0 model is reported as 2.5 times more efficient than the best frontier model.

The authors quantify evidence weights as Bayes factors to examine how models update beliefs over time, whether they agree with expert biologists on relevance, and where they show inconsistencies and biases.

gaps: Request the full text to check how the 2.5x efficiency figure and the baselines are defined and measured.
Request details on how expert biologist agreement on relevance was measured and on the reported inconsistencies and biases.
questions: Which reported results are measured benchmark outcomes versus proposed applications such as use in autonomous discovery?
Do the calibration gains hold on held-out domains or only on the three biological domains used here?
proposal: Retrieve the full paper to separate measured results (Brier scores, calibration, experiment-selection efficiency) from proposed downstream use.
